Situational cuing of materialism triggers self-objectification among women (but not men): The moderating role of self-concept clarity Fei Teng a,⁎, Kai-Tak Poon b, Hong Zhang c, Zhansheng Chen d, Ye Yang e, Xue Wang da School of Psychology, Center for Studies of Psychological Application, Guangdong Key Laboratory of Mental Health and Cognitive Science, The Base of Psychological Services and Counseling for “Happiness” in Guangzhou, South China Normal University, Guangzhou, China b Department of Psychology, The Hong Kong Institute of Education, Hong Kong c Department of Psychology, Nanjing University, Nanjing, China d Department of Psychology, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong e School of Humanities, Changshu Institute of Technology, Changshu, China article info abstract Article history: Received 14 October 2015 Received in revised form 17 March 2016 Accepted 20 March 2016 Available online xxxx The present research examined the influence of materialism on self-objectification among women. The results provided converging support to the prediction that experimentally priming materialistic belief would increase women's (but not men's) self-objectification tendency (Studies 1, 2 and 3). Moreover, Study 3 revealed that women's self-concept clarity moderated the effect of materialism on self-objectification tendency, such that only women with low self-concept clarity reported higher self-objectification tendencies following a materialism reminder. These findings contribute to the literature by highlighting the role played by societal ideology in women's development of self-objectification and also identifying a protective factor against such an effect. Implications for research on objectification, materialism as well as women's well-being were discussed. © 2016 Published by Elsevier Ltd. Keywords: Self-objectification Materialism Self-concept clarity Gender differences 1. Introduction A Fiat 500 Abarth car commercial portrayed a passionate story that a man encountered a seductive Italian woman, who turned into the new Fiat car at the end of the commercial; a group of blonde and big-breasted female models promoted Old Milwaukee beer in the famous Swedish Bikini Team campaign; an Abercrombie & Fitch women's slogan t-shirt said blatantly on the chest position, “Who needs a brain when you have these?” Seemingly unrelated, these advertisements promote material products in a way that subtly conveys the notion that women are valued on the basis of their bodies in a consumer society, unanimously suggesting a potential connection between materialism and a sexualized view of women. Although such a connection is implicated in advertisements, media portrayals and daily occurrences, it has never been empirically tested. The present research thus had two aims. First, it aimed to investigate this connection by examining whether materialism would increase women's adoption of a sexualized view upon themselves; and second, it aimed to identify a potential protective factor for such a negative effect, namely, whether self-concept clarity can weaken the effect of materialism on women's self-objectification tendency. 1.1.

Women who objectify themselves attach great importance to their appearance (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997) and often habitually monitor their outward appearance from an observational perspective (i.e., body surveillance; Lindberg, Hyde, & McKinley, 2006). Previous studies have accumulated evidence on the deleterious effect of self-objectification of women. . According to the objectification theory (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997), various situational factors can trigger self-objectification in women.

For example, women are more likely to sexually objectify themselves when putting on a revealing swimming suit while standing in front of a full-length mirror (Fredrickson et al., 1998), reading contemporary women's magazines (Tiggemann & McGill, 2004), overhearing weight or appearance commentaries (Calogero, Herbozo, & Thompson, 2009), and detecting or anticipating a male gaze (Calogero, 2004). These studies consistently demonstrated that situational cues that make physical appearance salient will lead to self-objectification. However, a more recent study conducted by Calogero and Jost (2011) found that incidental exposure to benevolent or complementary sexism can cause women to objectify themselves, suggesting that certain cultural ideology, in which physical appearance is not the main focus, can also trigger self-objectification. This research, therefore, highlights the need for situating self-objectification in a broader context of societal ideology. In the present research, we focused on a peculiar and socially prevalent ideology, namely, materialism, and we proposed that materialism can increase women's self-objectification tendency. 1.2. Materialism and self-objectification. Materialism is a value system, which is defined as ‘a set of centrally held beliefs about the importance of possessions in one's life’ (Richins & Dawson, 1992, p. 308). Such a value orientation encompasses the desire for a lifestyle associated with image, fame, and success, as well as on wealth and possessions. According to the consumer culture impact model (Dittmar, 2008), modern consumer society is featured by two interconnected ideals, which are “material good life” and “body perfect”, both of which represent a culturally-prescribed “ideal self”. Generally, these two sets of values are bounded together and perpetuated mainly by advertising. In fact, former content analyses of visual media (e.g., fashion magazines, television advertising, and programming) demonstrated the prevalence of images depicting products associated with young, tall, and extremely thin women who epitomize the current beauty ideal (Malkin, Wornian, & Chrisler, 1999; Fouts & Burggraf, 1999, 2000). Moreover, isolated body parts of women, such as a bare stomach, buttocks, cleavage, or a bare chest, are often depicted in commercial products (Kolbe & Albanese, 1996; Sommers-Flanagan, Sommers-Flanagan, & Davis, 1993), thereby communicating a sexualized view of women. According to Maio, Pakizeh, Cheung, and Rees (2009), when certain values are situationally activated, an ensemble of corresponding values are likely to be co-activated, while incompatible values are often inhibited (Maio et al., 2009).
To the extent that “material abundance” and “body perfect” are compatible and are associated closely with each other,

Our prediction that materialism may trigger self-objectification in women is consistent with prior research findings showing that reminders of materialism led female participants to be more dissatisfied about their bodies after viewing idealized body figures (Ashikali & Dittmar, 2011). This effect was especially salient among those high in materialistic value (Ashikali & Dittmar, 2011). However, due to the correlational nature of their study, a causal relationship between materialism and women's self-objectification cannot be established. Therefore, in the present research, we directly tested the impact of situational materialism on women's self-objectification and proposed that materialism would make women self-objectify themselves. 1.3. The moderating role of self-concept clarity People internalize culturally prevalent values to a different degree. Some people are more strongly influenced by cultural values, whereas others are more resilient to this kind of influence. Of particular interest in the present research are factors that could protect women from being influenced by the socially prevalent ideology, and we proposed that self-concept clarity is one such factor. Self-concept clarity is the structural aspect of self-concept which represents the extent to which knowledge components or specific self-beliefs are organized (Campbell, 1990). Generally, high self-concept clarity reflects a state that the content of self-concept (perceived self-attribute) is clearly organized, confidently defined, internally consistent, and temporally stable (Campbell, 1990; Campbell & Lavallee, 1993). Self-concept clarity is critical to people's daily functioning and health as research has found that a relative lack of clarity in self-concept correlates with global indicators of compromised functioning such as neuroticism, anxiety, and depression (Bigler, Neimeyer, & Brown, 2001; Campbell, 1990; Campbell, Assanand, & Di Paula, 2003; Campbell et al., 1996) as well as aggressive reactions to failure (Stucke & Spore, 2002). More importantly, Campbell (1990) posited that individuals with dif-ferent levels of self-concept clarity should respond differently towards external forces, such that people with low self-concept clarity “should be more dependent on, susceptible to, and influenced by external” forces (p. 539). Building upon Campbell's (1990) theory, people low in self-concept clarity should be more vulnerable to the influences of culturally-prescribed values. This proposition is sustained by a recent research conducted by Vartanian (2009), revealing a negative association between self-concept clarity and the internalization of cultural ideals of attractiveness among women. Furthermore, a more recent study demonstrated that self-concept clarity is negatively associated with both thin-ideal internalization and appearance-related social comparison tendencies, suggesting that self-concept clarity contributes to the vulnerability towards women's body image problems (Vartanian & Dey, 2013). There-fore, we predicted that self-concept clarity would moderate the effect of materialism on women's self-objectification inclination, such that materialism would trigger self-objectification among women low in self-concept clarity but not in women high in self-concept clarity. 2. Overview of the current study In the present research, we aimed to investigate the impact of materialism, as a situationally induced factor, on women's self- objectification. Following prior research (e.g., Calogero & Jost, 2011; Morris, Goldenberg, & Heflick, 2014; Harper & Tiggemann, 2008), self-objectification was assessed with the Self-objectification Scale by Noll and Fredrickson (1998) and the body-surveillance subscale of McKinley and Hyde's (1996) Objectified Body Consciousness Scale. The former scale reflects the importance people assign to appearance attributes (e.g., weight) as compared to competence attributes (e.g., health) in defining their physical self-concept, and the latter captures the extent to which people habitually monitor their outward appearance. We predicted that incidental exposure to materialism will increase women's self-objectification tendency (Studies 1 to 3). Moreover, we expected that self-concept clarity would moderate the relation between materialism and self-objectification tendency, such that the predicted effects would only emerge among women with low self-concept clarity, but not in women with high self-concept clarity (Study 3). 3. Study 1 In Study 1, we directly tested the casual relationship between materialism and self-objectification variables in a sample of Chinese women. China has witnessed a great growth in its economic status as well as its participation in the global market. Rapid increases in the consumption of luxury goods imply that materialistic values are gaining power in its F. Teng et al. / Personality and Individual Differences 97 (2016) 220–228 221 influences on Chinese people. According to a survey conducted by a global research firm (IPSOS) across 20 countries, 71% of Chinese said that they gauge their success by the things they own. This percentage was significantly higher than that of any other nation in the world (IPSOS, 2013). Moreover, Wei and Talpade (2009) found that, overall, Chinese mature consumers are more materialistic than their American counterparts; and this effect was replicated in young Chinese consumers as well (Podoshen, Li, & Zhang, 2011). The prosperity of consumerism in China is also associated with the strict beauty standards as well as the objectifying perspective on women. By analyzing data from the Miss Hong Kong Beauty Pageant from 1975 to 2000, Leung and colleagues demonstrated that thinness and big waist to hip ratio were highly looked up upon in Chinese culture (Leung, Lam, & Sze, 2001). This beauty standard has been propagandized by media and communicated by parents or peers to women (Chen & Jackson, 2012) which makes Chinese women become increasingly dissatisfied about their bodies and constantly engage in the beautification of their outer appearances (Chen & Jackson, 2012; Jackson & Chen., 2007). In fact, for the past 20 years, a beauty economy-based largely on the production and consumption of feminine beauty, youth, and appearance — has risen to become China's third largest growth industry behind real estate and tourism (Luo, 2013). Yang (2011) maintains that objectifying societal changes have resulted in Chinese women's bodies becoming sources of increased scrutiny and those deemed to be defective are targeted for modification.

Following prior research (Bauer, Wilkie, Kim, & Bodenhausen, 2012), we presented female participants with advertisements of luxury products (vs. ordinary products) to activate the materialism belief, and then measured their state self-objectification and level of body-surveillance. Moreover, past research showed that self-objectified women are more inclined to engage in appearance management (e.g., dieting, undertaking cosmetic surgery) in order to bring them- selves in line with cultural body ideals (e.g., Fredrickson et al., 1998; Calogero, Pina, Park, & Rahemtulla, 2010). Therefore, in the present research, we also measured participants' appearance management intention as indicated by their purchasing tendency for appearance-related products (e.g., slimming clothes). We expected participants to report a greater tendency to objectify themselves after viewing the materialistic advertisements, and that their self-objectification tendency would mediate the effect of materialism on appearance management. 3.1. Methods 3.1.1. Participants Sixty-three female undergraduate students from a university in China (mean age = 21.08, SD = 1.07) participated in exchange for a small amount of monetary reward. Participants were recruited using flyers posted on the campus. They were randomly assigned to either the materialism condition or the control condition. 3.1.2. Procedures Participants made appointments with the experimenter through email and went to a psychological lab to participate in the experiment during their assigned timeslots. We had told the participants in the advertisements that they would complete several unrelated tests during the experiment, including general personality tests and consumer attitudes, before they agreed to participate in this study. Upon arrival to the laboratory, participants' informed consent was obtained, and they were asked to work on a media evaluation task where they were instructed to evaluate several advertisements. Specifically, participants were presented with 3 pieces of advertisements, each of which was shown on a computer screen for 2 min. Participants were instructed to evaluate each advertisement for their clarity and level of fun. To manip- ulate materialism orientation, participants in the materialism group watched advertisements about luxury products (i.e., a luxury car, a luxury watch, and a luxury house); whereas participants in the control group viewed advertisements for more frugal versions of products in the same categories (i.e., an economical car, a cheap watch, and a budget apartment). To avoid priming people with idealized body images, which was found to be able to induce a state of self-objectification in previous research (Harper & Tiggemann, 2008), we did not include any images of women nor men in the advertisements. Moreover, we removed trade-marks from all the advertisements to avoid arousing any pre-existing attitudes or feelings towards different brands. Afterwards, to check the effectiveness of the manipulation, participants answered two items about their material beliefs based on their current feelings on a 7-point scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree). The two items were: “I want a lot of luxury in my life” and “Owning material things can make me happy”(r= .46, p b .001). Next, participants completed measures of self-objectification variables.1 The measures included the body-surveillance subscale of the Objectified Body Consciousness Scale (McKinley & Hyde, 1996) and Self-objectification Scale (SOQ; Noll & Fredrickson, 1998). The body-surveillance subscale measures the extent to which people habit-ually monitor their outward appearance from an observational stand-point. Participants were instructed to rate eight items on a 7-point scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree). A sample item is “During the day, I think about how I look many times”. Mean scores were calculated to provide an index of body-surveillance, with higher scores indicating more body-surveillance. This scale has been widely used in prior research and has demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity in Chinese samples (Jackson & Chen, 2015; α = .89 in the present sample). SOQ measures the degree to which people value their physical appearance as compared to their physical competence. Specifically, participants were asked to rank 10 body attributes in the order of their importance in defining their physical self-concept. Five of the attributes were appearance-related (i.e., weight, sexuality, body measurements, appearances, and muscle strength), whereas the other five were competence-related (i.e., health, strength, energy level, physical coordination, and physical fitness). The difference scores were calculated by subtracting the sum of competence scores from the sum of appearances scores, and a higher score on this scale indicates a greater focus on physical appearance in comparison with physical competence. The reliability of SOQ was determined by correlating the sum of the appearance ranks and the sum of the competence ranks (Hill & Fischer, 2008; Calogero & Jost, 2011) and the correlation coefficient was −.99 in the present sample, indicating satisfactory reliability. Furthermore, we modified the instructions of the two scales to capture participants' momentary states by asking participants to report their current feelings. Finally, participants were presented with three pictures of appearance-related products (i.e., slimming clothes, perfume, a hair curler) and three pictures of control products 2 (i.e., a computer accessory, earphones, office stationery). Results and discussion All dependent variables were analyzed using a one-way ANOVA, with materialism as the between-subject variable. 3.2.1. Manipulation check Participants were more materialistic in the materialism condition (M = 5.09, SD = 1.21) than in the control condition (M = 3.96, SD = 1.45), F(1,61) = 10.19, p b .01, ηp 2 = .14. Therefore, our manipulation was successful. 3.2.2. Body-surveillance There was a main effect of materialism, F(1,61) = 10.54, p b .01, ηp 2 = .15, such that female participants reported greater body- surveillance in the materialism condition (M = 4.84, SD = .77) than in the control condition (M = 4.13, SD = .89). 3.2.3. State self-objectification The results showed that materialism exerted a significant main effect on state self-objectification, F(1,61) = 5.62, p = .02, ηp 2 = .08. Specifically, women who viewed advertisements of luxury products reported higher scores (M = −8.33, SD = 8.88) than those who viewed ordinary products in the Self-objectification Scale (M = −13.33, SD = 7.64). 3.2.4. Appearance management A repeated measures ANOVA with materialism priming as a between-subject variable and product type as a within-subject variable revealed a significant interaction between priming and product type, F(1,61) = 4.13, p b .05, ηp 2 = .06, however, neither the main effect of priming nor product type were statistically significant, Fs b 1.68, ps N .20. To clarify the nature of the expected interaction effect, we conducted a series of planned a priori comparisons. Specifically, simple effect analyses showed that there was a main effect of materialism on purchasing tendencies for appearance-related products, F(1,61) = 4.55, p = .04 ,ηp 2 = .07, such that female participants in the materialism condition re-ported greater willingness to purchase the appearance-related products (M = 4.14, SD = 1.47) than those in the control condition (M = 3.19, SD = 1.85). However, the effect was not observed on ordinary products between materialism primed participants (M = 3.45, SD = 1.31) and those assigned to the control condition (M = 3.55, SD = 1.67), F(1,61) = .02, p = .88. 3.2.5. Mediation analysis Using procedures recommended by Preacher and Hayes (2004), we treated the independent variable as the predictor, body-surveillance and state self-objectification as mediators, and appearance management as the criterion variable. This analysis revealed a significant indirect effect for body-surveillance (with 5000 iterations, bias corrected, and accelerated 95% confidence interval = .03 to .54). Inclusion of this mediator reduced the uncorrected experimental effect (b = .26, p = .04) to non-significance (b = .14, p = .29) (see Fig. 1), suggesting that participant's body-surveillance accounted for the effect of materialism on appearance management. However, the indirect effect of state self-objectification was not statistically significant (with 5000 iterations, bias corrected, and accelerated 95% confidence interval = −.27 to.05). Study 1 provided primary evidence that materialism cues are environmental triggers for self-objectification in women. Specifically, we found that women had an increased tendency to objectify themselves following exposure to materialism reminders, as indicated by an increased degree of body-surveillance and heightened importance assigned to appearance. Moreover, the increased body-surveillance mediated the effect of materialism on women's appearance management intentions. State self-objectification did not serve as a mediator in the relation between materialism and appearance management. This effect is in line with past research. In fact, although both body-surveillance and self-objectification demonstrated acceptable reliability and validity in previous studies, body-surveillance was shown to be more reliable in predicting criterion variables in the present study. Specifically, when self-objectification and body-surveillance were considered together, body-surveillance typically emerged as a variable uniquely related to the criterion variables while self-objectification did not (e.g., Greenleaf & McGreer, 2006; Szymanski & Henning, 2007; Calogero & Jost, 2011). 4. Study 2 In study 2, we aimed to replicate the findings of Study 1 in a U.S. sample. Moreover, we adopted another paradigm to manipulate the concept of materialism in order to increase the validity of the findings in Study 1. Following prior research (Bauer et al., 2012), we presented participants with pictures of luxury products to activate the materialism belief, and then measured self-objectification related variables. Furthermore, we also examined whether the effect of materialism on women's self-objectification can be extended to men. Previous studies showed that men will objectify themselves in certain circumstances. For example, when putting on a speedo swimsuit and standing in front of a mirror, men reported increased feelings of self-objectification (Martins, Tiggemann, & Kirkbride, 2007).

Teng et al. / Personality and Individual Differences 97 (2016) 220–228 223 4.1. Methods 4.1.1. Participants One hundred and eighty-one participants (90 males and 91 females) from America participated in our study on Amazon Mechanical Turk (Buhrmester, Kwang, & Gosling, 2011) in exchange for a small amount of monetary reward. Participants were recruited using advertisements posted on Amazon Mechanical Turk. We had told the participants in the advertisements that they would complete several unrelated tests during the experiment, including general personality tests and a media evaluation task, before they agreed to participate in this study. The mean age of the participants was 37.22 years old (SD = 12.88) and the ethnic composition of the sample was: 81.2% were Caucasian, 6.1% were Asian, 5.5% were African, 3.9% were Hispanic, and 3.3% did not identify their ethnicity. 4.1.2. Procedures and materials After signing a consent form, participants were led to believe that they would complete several unrelated tasks to minimize their knowledge of our research hypotheses. First, participants were instructed to work on a picture evaluation task. Specifically, they were asked to evaluate 20 pictures,3 the presentation order of which was randomized. Participants were instructed to evaluate each picture in terms of their clarity and structure. To manipulate materialism, participants in the materialism condition viewed pictures depicting luxury products (e.g., a luxury car, luxury furniture); whereas participants in the control group viewed pictures of ordinary products (e.g., paper, an ordinary chair). To control possible confounding effects, none of the pictures included any images of women and men. Next, participants completed the same manipulation check questions used in Studies 1 and 2. Specifically, they rated the extent to which they agreed to each of the two statements “I want a lot of luxury in my life” and “Owning material things can make me happy” (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree; r = .40, p b .001). Finally, participants completed the body- surveillance subscale (α = .80) as well as the SOQ (r = −.97, p b .001) used in Study 1. To fit the research purpose of this study, participants were asked to complete the two scales based on their current feelings. After completing all the above tasks, participants were instructed to provide their demographic information, and were then directed to a funneled debriefing page. 4.2. Results and discussion All dependent variables were analyzed using a two-way ANOVA, with materialism and gender as the between-subject variables. 4.2.1. Manipulation check Participants were more materialistic in the materialism priming condition (M = 4.22, SD = 1.66) than in the control condition (M = 3.66, SD = 1.54), F(1,177) = 4.51, p b .05, ηp 2 = .03. The interaction between materialism and gender was not significant, F(1,177) = 1.72, p = .19. Therefore, our manipulation was effective. 4.2.2. Body-surveillance There was a main effect of gender, F(1,177) = 10.78, p = .001, ηp 2 = .06, such that female participants scored higher on the body-surveillance scale (M = 4.07, SD = 1.23) than male participants (M = 3.59, SD = 1.28). The main effect of materialism was not significant, F(1,177) = .13, p = .72, More importantly, the interaction of condition and gender was significant, F(1,177) = 7.62, p b .01, ηp 2 = .04. To clarify the nature of the expected interaction effect, we conducted a series of planned a priori comparisons. Specifically, simple effects tests demonstrated that female participants scored higher on body-surveillance in the materialism condition (M = 4.42, SD = 1. 32) than in the control condition (M = 3.82, SD = 1. 11), F(1,177) = 5.30, p = .02, ηp 2 = .06; however, male participants did not differ on body- surveillance between the materialism condition (M = 3.25, SD = 1.08) and the control condition (M = 3.72, SD = 1.33), F(1,177) = 2.66, p = .10. Further tests showed that female participants reported more surveillance (M = 4.42, SD = 1. 32) than male participants after a materialism reminder, F(1,177) = 13.88, p b .001, ηp 2 = .07; and this effect was not observed in the control condition, F(1,177) = .19, p = .66. 4.2.3. State self-objectification The main effect of gender was marginally significant, F(1,177) = 3.71, p = .05. ηp 2 = .02, such that female participants reported greater state self-objectification (M = 4.38, SD = 14.22) than male participants(M = 1.84, SD = 14.34). The main effect of materialism was not significant, F(1,177) = 2.32, p = .14, More importantly, the interaction of condition and gender was significant, F(1,177) = 4.01, p = .04, ηp 2 =.02. To clarify the nature of the expected interaction effect, we conducted a series of planned a priori comparisons. Specifically, simple effect analyses demonstrated that female participants scored higher on self-objectification in the materialism condition (M = 9.92, SD = 12. 53) than in the control condition (M = 2.13, SD = 13. 97), F(1,177) = 5.65, p = .02, ηp 2 = .03; however, male participants did not differ on self-objectification between the materialism condition (M = 1.16, SD = 12.13) and the control condition (M = 2.30, SD = 15.77), F(1,177) = .14, p = .71. Further tests showed that female participants reported more self-objectification than male participants after a materialism reminder, F(1,177) = 5.87, p = .02, ηp 2 = .03; and this effect was not observed in the control condition, F(1,177) = .004, p = .94.  Our second study provided further evidence about the association between materialism orientation and self-objectification inclination in a U.S. sample. Moreover, we found that situational reminders of materialism can trigger self-objectification tendencies in women but not in men. This effect is consistent with past research showing that environmental and interpersonal triggers of women's self-objectification usually do not lead to the same effects in men. 5. Study 3 In Study 3, we aimed to replicate the patterns we found in Studies 1 and 2. More importantly, we investigated whether self-concept clarity could buffer the effect of materialism cues on women's self-objectification related variables. We predicted that materialism would increase women's tendency to objectify themselves among those low in self-concept clarity, but not among those with high self-concept clarity. 5.1. Methods 5.1.1. Participants Nighty-eight female undergraduate students from a university in China (mean age = 22.11, SD = 1.23) participated in exchange for a small amount of monetary reward. Participants were recruited using flyers posted on campus. Procedures Participants made appointments with the experimenter through email and went to a psychological lab in their assigned timeslots. After written consents were provided, participants were told to perform several alleged unrelated tasks. First, participants completed the 12-item Self-concept Clarity Scale (Campbell et al., 1996). On 7-point scales (1 = totally disagree;7= totally agree), participants indicated the extent to which they agreed on 12 statements. A sample item is “My beliefs about myself seem to change very frequently.” This scale was translated into Chinese by the first author and then it was back-translated into English by a bilingual Psychology professor. Modifications were made until the authors agreed that the back translation matched the meaning of the original English version. Mean scores were calculated to index the clarity of self-concept, with higher scores indicating higher levels of clarity (α = .81). Afterwards, similar to Study 2, participants were instructed to work on a media image evaluation task. Specifically, 20 pictures were presented on a computer screen, with each shown for 2 s. Participants were asked to evaluate each picture in terms of its clarity and structure. To manipulate materialism orientation, all the pictures presented to participants in the materialism condition were about luxury products. Participants in the control group viewed pictures about natural scenes. The pictures were the same as those used in Study 2. Next, participants completed the same manipulation check questions as used in Studies 1and 2 (r = .48, p b .001). Finally, participants completed the body surveillance subscale (α = .81) and the SOQ (r = −.99) used in Studies 1 and 2. Participants were then asked to provide their demographic information, and were then debriefed before leaving.5.2. Results and discussion 5.2.1. Manipulation check Female participants were more materialistic in the materialism priming condition (M = 4.78, SD = 1.07) than in the control condition (M = 3.34, SD = 1.26), F(1,96) = 12.44, p b .001, ηp 2 = .12. Therefore, our manipulation was effective. 5.2.2. Body surveillance We regressed participants' body-surveillance onto the materialism condition (control = −1, materialism = 1), perceived self-concept clarity (mean-centered), and the two-way interaction. The results revealed a significant main effect of materialism, b = .20, t(94) = 2.12, p = .04; and a main effect of self-concept clarity, b = −.24, t(94) = −2.57, p = .01. More importantly, the two-way interaction between materialism and self-concept clarity was significant, b = −.22, t(94) = −2.32, p = .02 (R2 = .17; see Fig. 2). To clarify the nature of the expected interaction effect, we con-ducted a series of planned a priori comparisons. Specifically, follow-up simple slope analyses were conducted to determine group differences. Among participants low in self-concept clarity (1 SD below the mean), participants in the materialism condition exhibited greater body-surveillance than participants in the control condition did, b = .42, t(94) = 3.08, p b .01. However, participants high in self-concept clarity (1 SD above the mean) did not differ between the materialism condition and the control condition on body-surveillance, b = −.02, t(94) = −.14, p = .89. Furthermore, among participants in the materialism condition, self-concept clarity was negatively associated with body-surveillance, b = −.49, t(45) = −3.78, p b .001. This association was not observed among participants in the control condition, b = −.02, t(49) = −.16, p = .87. 5.2.3. State self-objectification. Study 3 provided further evidence that materialism is a powerful environmental stimulus that will increase women's tendency to objectify themselves. Moreover, we found that self-concept clarity moderated this relation between materialism and women's body-surveillance, such that only women low in self-concept clarity exhibited heightened body-surveillance after a materialism reminder. These findings suggest that self-concept clarity could protect women against the negative influences of environmental pressures. However, we did not find any moderation effect of self-concept clarity on the relation between materialism and state self-objectification. This might be because the SOQ and the body-surveillance scale captured different aspects of self-objectification. Self-concept clarity can moderate the effect of materialism on women's behavioral intentions (i.e., actively monitor their body from an observational perspective) but not on women's perception of self-attributes (i.e., the assigned im- portance to appearance relative to fitness) as a whole. This effect also suggests the possibility that women's sexualized views of themselves are harder to modulate than that of their behavioral intentions. 6. General discussion In modern consumer society, popular media is overwhelmed by advertisements in which women are portrayed in a sexualized way, implicitly suggesting a connection between material possessions and a perfect body figure. We proposed that materialism is an environmental trigger of self-objectification for women, insofar as material abundance and a perfect body are socially valued ideals that connected to each other closely (Dittmar, 2008). Experimental evidence converged to support our proposition. Specifically, we situationally induced materialism belief by letting participants watch advertisements of luxury products or by presenting participants with pictures depicting luxury products in the three studies, and we found that situationally-induced materialism increased women's endorsement of a sexually-objectified perspective on themselves. This program of research provides the first experimental evidence that mere reminders of materialism will make women more inclined to objectify themselves. Prior research demonstrated that women exhibit increased tendency for self-objectification in situations where their body is made salient (e.g., Fredrickson et al., 1998; Tiggemann & Fig. 2. The present research contributes to the objectification theory by showing that certain situational cues that do not contain any explicit information about the physical body could give rise to self-objectification. Our findings that materialism triggers self-objectification tendencies in women are in congruence with past research findings showing that materialism increases women's dissatisfaction about their body (Ashikali & Dittmar, 2011). We take this line of research a step further by drawing a link between materialism and self-objectification directly, thereby suggesting the possibility that women's increased dissatisfaction about their bodies might be due to an increased degree of self-objectification. Materialism exerts deleterious effects on people (for a review, seeKasser, 2002). Generally, materialistic people report lower self-esteem (Ryan et al., 1999), more negative affect (Christopher & Schlenker, 2004), and lower levels of well-being (e.g. Kasser & Ahuvia, 2002; Kasser & Ryan, 1993). However, women seem to be more vulnerable to the influences of materialism than men. A meta-analytical study found that, the link between materialism and lower well-being is stronger when women make up a greater proportion of the respondents (Dittmar, Bond, Hurst, & Kasser, 2014). Our research findings, therefore, could shed light on this line of research by pointing out the possibility that materialism inflicts its detrimental impacts especially on women

and through, at least partially, increasing women's self-objectification. The mechanism underlying materialism and self-objectification is contingent self-valuation. For materialists, their self-worth rests on material possessions and money they own; for self-objectifiers, their worth lies on the attractiveness and sexuality of their appearances. In a modern consumerist society, these two sets of values are interconnected and perpetuated together by advertisements emphasizing women's bodies. Having established the impact of materialism on women's self- objectification, the obvious next step would be to investigate the impact of self-objectification on people's attitudes towards material possession and acquisition. Will self-objectified women exhibit stronger desires for materials and money? Will self-objectified women pursue extrinsic financial goals at the expense of intrinsic psychological needs? Answers to these questions could help to better understand the influences of sexual objectification on women. In Study 1 we found that women increases appearance- management endeavors through purchasing appearance-related products as a response to a materialism reminder. Our research, therefore, provides insights for understanding women's consumption behaviors. For example, research showed that people engage in compulsive consumption, which refers to the tendency of excessively buying things at the expense

of psychological health and financial security (Dittmar, 2004b). This trend is especially salient among women (see reviews by Black, 2004; Faber, 2004). Researchers believed that compulsive buying could be conceived of as a type of compensatory consumption whereby people deal with their identity problems in a materialistic society (Dittmar, 2004b; Elliott, 1994). It is thus plausible that the prevailing materialism values in a consumerist society increase women's concerns on their appearance, coaxing them into buying products which would bring them in line with the culturally-prescribed identity - a woman possessing a perfect body. Therefore, our research helps to understand the deleterious impact of materialism on women, and open up possibilities for future intervention programs targeting women's overall well-being and health. In Study 3, we found that individual differences in self-concept clarity affected how women responded to materialism, such that body-surveillance efforts were greater among low self-concept clarity women but weaker among high self-concept clarity women following exposure to materialism. According to Campbell (1990), self-concept clarity influences the extent to which people internalize cultural values, with low self-concept clarity individuals more strongly subjected to environmental pressures. That is, low self-concept clarity individuals may seek external information to define themselves or form their identities due to a lack of a clear sense of who they really are. Therefore, women with low self-concept clarity would be more likely to internalize the culturally prescriptive ideals or make themselves become in line with the cultural ideal. In contrast, high self-concept clarity women did not show this effect, suggesting that self-concept clarity could somehow protect women against the negative consequences of materialism, which may otherwise be hard to resist. Given that a large part of the negative impacts of sexual objectification on women arises from women's internalization of an observational perspective on the self and view one's self through an objectified lens (for a review, see Moradi & Huang, 2008), our research provide possibilities for intervention programs. Specifically, if self-concept clarity could protect women from conforming to culturally prevalent ideologies, it is possible that self-concept clarity could play a role in helping women deal with other negative outcomes of sexual objectification. Thus, self-concept clarity appears to be a critical variable to consider in future investigations of sexual objectification. It should be noted that although state self-objectification and body-surveillance are both regarded as indexes of the tendency for women to objectify themselves, they exert their influences differently and respond differently to the potential protecting factor. For example, body-surveillance, but not state self-objectification, can serve as a mediator in the relation between materialism and appearance management. Moreover, self-concept clarity can moderate the relation between materialism and body-surveillance (but not self-objectification). We think the different pattern of results might be because the SOQ and the body-surveillance scale capture different aspects of self-objectification. Specifically, body-surveillance is more of a reflection of women's behavioral intentions (i.e., actively monitor their body from an observational perspective), whereas state self-objectification is about women's perception of self-attributes (i.e., the assigned importance to appearance relative to fitness). It is, thus, worthy of further investigation to further differentiate these two constructs as well as the way they exert their peculiar influences on women. In sum, by building up the connection between materialism and women's self-objectification, the present research provides a crucial foundation for understanding the deleterious effect of materialism on women's general well-being and mental health. We hope it marks a new avenue for future research into the details of the link between materialism and self-objectification as well as the potential reciprocal nature of their relationship. The moderating effect of self-concept clarity upon their relation also sheds lights on future intervention programs targeting women struggling in the contemporary consumer society. Moreover, our research contributes to literature on self-objectification by providing cross-cultural evidence on the prevalence of this phenomenon. Previous research on self-objectification has emphasized western women of European heritage; however, the body image issue is not culture-bounded.

Moreover, recent research has provided some evidence showing that objectification influences people from the western and eastern cultures similarly. In particular, both Chinese and American women tend to avoid interacting with men following sexual objectification (Saguy et al., 2010; Teng et al., 2015).

In the present research, we further demonstrated that situational materialism can increase both Chinese and American women's self-objectification tendency. Nevertheless, future research should devote more effort to investigate the development of self-objectification and its effects on women's mental and physical health in different cultures.  Our study was not without limitations which could open avenues for future research. Specifically, we used women's purchasing tendency for appearance related products as an index of their motivation for 226 F. Teng et al. / Personality and Individual Differences 97 (2016) 220–228 appearance management. However, purchasing tendency might be part in measuring some aspect of consumerism as participants were asked about “purchasing” the product. Although previous research demonstrated that individuals' psychological needs and behavioral intentions can be reflected in the products that they would like to choose or pur-chase (e.g., Zhong & Liljenquist, 2006; Chen et al., 2013), this measure is not as direct as an index of appearance management intention, such as the acceptance of cosmetic surgery, used in previous studies (Calogero et al., 2010). Therefore, future research should consider using more direct measures of women's appearance management intentions and behaviors. Moreover, although the measures of self-objectification tendency indicated satisfactory reliability in the present Chinese samples, they need to be validated in more broad Chinese samples due to the different cultural, political, and economic contexts in China.
